about: Evidence grade for each modifiable factor the app can change. strongest_design is the strongest design that estimates an effect of the factor on divorce or separation; evidence entries are copied from the verified evidence files.

factors.label: Age / timing of marriage
factors.decision: Timing a marriage: marrying later rather than sooner
app_inputs: age at marriage (from ages and years married)
couple what-if: timing of the wedding
factors.direction: later marriage, lower risk (steepest below the early twenties, flattening after about 25-28)
factors.size: Teen marriage roughly doubles or more the hazard relative to marrying in the early-to-mid twenties (adjusted HR 2.42 for 18 or younger vs 22-24; this project 2.63 at 17 vs about 23). Beyond the late twenties the gains are small.
factors.causal_reading: Consistent across many cohorts and surveys after adjustment, so waiting past the teens and early twenties is a reasonable bet, but no experiment or instrument estimates the effect on divorce itself. The only quasi-experimental study (state marriage-age laws) shows teen marriage causes later poverty, not divorce.
factors.gaps: No quasi-experimental estimate of age at marriage on divorce found; selection (maturity, partner quality, pregnancy) remains plausible.

evidence.title: Rising women's age at marriage and the fall in US divorce
evidence.effect_text: Older ages at marriage are the main proximate cause of falling divorce among post-1980 marriages.
evidence.design: Three empirical approaches across SIPP, NLSY79 and NSFG (per the abstract); not randomised
evidence.population: US women marrying after 1980
evidence.citation: Rotz, D. (2016). Why have divorce rates fallen? The role of women's age at marriage. Journal of Human Resources, 51(4), 961-1002.
evidence.quote: Three different empirical approaches suggest that the increase in women’s age at marriage is the main proximate cause of the fall in divorce rates.
evidence.caveats: "Proximate cause" is the author's term; designs are observational. Abstract only.

evidence.title: Early teen marriage instrumented by state minimum-age-at-marriage, schooling and work laws
evidence.measure: IV effect on poverty, percentage points
evidence.effect_text: Marrying as a young teen raised the chance of later poverty by 31 percentage points (IV); dropping out of school by 11 points.
evidence.design: Instrumental variables using state laws on marriage age, school leaving and work age
evidence.population: US women (Census microdata)
evidence.outcome: Living in poverty later in life (NOT divorce)
evidence.citation: Dahl, G. B. (2010). Early teen marriage and future poverty. Demography, 47(3), 689-718.
evidence.quote: The baseline IV estimate indicates that a woman who marries young is 31 percentage points more likely to live in poverty when she is older.
evidence.caveats: Outcome is poverty, not divorce; applies to very early (teen) marriage in older cohorts. No quasi-experimental estimate of age at marriage on divorce itself was found.

factors.label: Finishing education (degree before marriage)
factors.decision: Finishing a degree before marrying; choosing a partner by education
factors.size: A bachelor's degree is associated with roughly 30-40% lower hazard after adjustment (this project 0.63; Killewald 2016: wife 0.71, husband 0.57).
factors.causal_reading: Robust association; how much is education itself versus the traits and circumstances that lead to college is not identified.
factors.gaps: No natural-experiment estimate of schooling on divorce found.

factors.label: Living together before marriage
factors.decision: Cohabiting first, and whether to do so before or after engagement
app_inputs: couple what-if: live together / do not
factors.direction: near null in recent cohorts; higher risk mainly for cohabiting before a commitment to marry or with several prior partners
factors.size: Adjusted estimates range from about no difference (this project 1.01, adjusted; Manning & Cohen 1.03, zero-order) to modestly higher (Killewald 2016: OR 1.29); cohabiting after engagement 0.57.
factors.causal_reading: No randomised or natural-experiment evidence. A selection model finds dissolution-prone people select into cohabiting, and adjusted estimates shrink toward zero in recent cohorts, so cohabiting itself is unlikely to change risk much. In the Army PREP trial, couples who had cohabited before committing divorced more only without the programme.
factors.gaps: No experiment or instrument on cohabitation timing found.

evidence.title: Premarital cohabitation with selection into cohabiting modelled jointly
evidence.effect_text: Evidence that more dissolution-prone people select into cohabiting; the raw cohabitation-divorce link is partly selection.
evidence.design: Joint hazard model with correlated unobserved heterogeneity across the cohabit and divorce decisions
evidence.population: National Longitudinal Study of the High School Class of 1972
evidence.citation: Lillard, L. A., Brien, M. J., & Waite, L. J. (1995). Premarital cohabitation and subsequent marital dissolution: A matter of self-selection? Demography, 32(3), 437-457.
evidence.quote: We find significant heterogeneity in both cohabitation and marriage disruption, and discover evidence of self-selection into cohabitation.
evidence.caveats: Identification rests on model assumptions, not randomisation; older cohort when cohabiting was uncommon. Abstract only.

evidence.title: Divorce by cohabitation history within each arm of the Army PREP trial
evidence.measure: risk difference (cohabited before commitment minus did not), control arm
evidence.effect_text: Without PREP, couples who had cohabited before committing to marry divorced more (14.6% vs 7.5%); with PREP there was no difference (7.8% vs 7.4%).
evidence.design: Secondary analysis of the Army PREP RCT: cohabitation history (not randomised) as a moderator of the randomised intervention
evidence.population: Married U.S. Army couples (Army PREP trial)
evidence.n: 309 control and 329 PREP couples with cohabitation history
evidence.outcome: Filed for divorce by 2 years, by whether the couple lived together before a mutual commitment to marry
evidence.citation: Rhoades, G. K., Stanley, S. M., Markman, H. J., & Allen, E. S. (2015). Can marriage education mitigate the risks associated with premarital cohabitation? Journal of Family Psychology, 29(3), 500-506.
evidence.quote: A significant chi-square test in the control group showed that 18 out of 123 (14.6%) of those who cohabited before a mutual commitment to marry filed for divorce compared to 14 out of 186 (7.5%) of those who did not, χ2 (1, N = 309) = 4.03, p < .05. For the PREP group, there was not a significant difference in divorce by cohabitation history, with 11 out of 141 (7.8%) of those who cohabited before a mutual commitment to marry having filed for divorce compared to 14 out of 188 (7.4%) of those who did not, χ2 (1, N = 329) = 0.02, p = .90.
evidence.caveats: Cohabitation history is self-selected and reported years after the fact; only the intervention is randomised. Subgroup contrast, not a test of cohabiting itself.

factors.label: Income and employment
factors.decision: Job stability, earnings, and income support
factors.direction: mixed: job loss raises risk modestly; extra income alone shows little effect
factors.size: Welfare work-incentive trial: −3.5 points divorce over 7 years for two-parent recipient families, none for applicants. Plant-closure job loss: +18% (CI includes no effect) in Sweden, no detectable effect in the US; lottery windfalls of $25-50k: no change. Prospective: husband full-time employment OR 0.75; income per $1,000 OR 1.00.
factors.causal_reading: Randomised and natural-experiment evidence exists but is narrow. It does not support 'more money, fewer divorces' as a general rule; a husband's employment matters more than income in prospective data.
factors.gaps: Experimental evidence limited to low-income welfare populations; no trial of earnings for middle-income couples.

evidence.title: Minnesota Family Investment Program (financial work incentives, simplified welfare) vs AFDC
evidence.effect_text: 10.4% of MFIP vs 13.8% of AFDC recipient families divorced (−3.5 points, about −25%, p < .05); among new applicants divorce was not lower (21.0% vs 18.8%, n.s.).
evidence.design: Randomised welfare-policy trial; divorce from state certificate records over about 7 years
evidence.population: Two-parent families receiving welfare (recipients) in 7 Minnesota counties
evidence.citation: Gennetian, L. A., & Knox, V. (2003). The long-term effects of the Minnesota Family Investment Program on marriage and divorce among two-parent families. New York: MDRC (prepared for ASPE, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services).
evidence.quote: Recipient familiesb 1,515 10.4 13.8 -3.5 ** -25.0
evidence.caveats: Effect only among long-term recipients, not applicants; one state; the policy bundle changed income, work and rules together. No CI printed.

evidence.title: Seattle-Denver Income-Maintenance Experiment (negative income tax) vs AFDC
evidence.effect_text: Contested: Cain & Wissoker found no effect of the negative income tax plans on dissolution; Hannan & Tuma found increases for Black and white (not Chicano) couples.
evidence.design: Randomised income-maintenance experiment; two published reanalyses disagree
evidence.population: Low-income husband-wife families in Seattle and Denver
evidence.citation: Cain, G. G., & Wissoker, D. A. (1990). A reanalysis of marital stability in the Seattle-Denver Income-Maintenance Experiment. American Journal of Sociology, 95(5), 1235-1269; Hannan, M. T., & Tuma, N. B. (1990). A reassessment of the effect of income maintenance on marital dissolution in the Seattle-Denver experiment. American Journal of Sociology, 95(5), 1270-1298.
evidence.quote: The conclusion of this paper is that the plans (specifically, the negative income tax plans in the experiment) had no effect on the rate of marital dissolutions among the "treatment" couples relative to the control couples.
evidence.caveats: Same data, opposite conclusions depending on treatment definitions and attrition handling.

evidence.title: Job loss through an establishment closure (Sweden)
evidence.effect_text: Divorce about 18% higher in the year of a closure-induced job loss, for either spouse, but the 95% intervals include no effect; a second rise followed the early-1990s recession.
evidence.design: Establishment closures in 1987 with a propensity-score-matched comparison group, Swedish registers
evidence.population: All married couples in Sweden where one spouse was displaced by a closure, plus matched comparisons
evidence.n: all displaced married workers in 1987 closures (register data)
evidence.outcome: Divorce in the year of the job loss
evidence.citation: Eliason, M. (2012). Lost jobs, broken marriages. Journal of Population Economics, 25(4), 1365-1397.
evidence.quote: There is an immediate increase, in the relative risk of divorce, of 18 percent (CIM: 0.81-1.49, CIW: 0.88-1.43) from both husbands’ and wives’ job losses.
evidence.caveats: Immediate-year CIs include 1. Working-paper version read; published 2012.

evidence.title: Husband's job loss from a plant closure (exogenous) vs a layoff
evidence.measure: probit coefficient, husband's plant closure 1-3 years ago
evidence.effect_text: Job loss from a plant closure: no detectable change in divorce (probit −0.149, SE 0.165). Layoffs (which may reveal something about the worker) raised divorce in the next 1-3 years (0.309, SE 0.095).
evidence.design: Panel probit of divorce on job-loss events, distinguishing plant closures (plausibly exogenous to the worker) from layoffs
evidence.population: Married couples, Panel Study of Income Dynamics (SRC subsample)
evidence.outcome: Marriage ends in divorce by next year
evidence.follow_up: up to 5+ years after job loss
evidence.citation: Charles, K. K., & Stephens, M., Jr. (2004). Job displacement, disability, and divorce. Journal of Labor Economics, 22(2), 489-522.
evidence.quote: Reason for Husband's Job Plant Closed: 1-3 Years Ago -0.149 0.165
evidence.caveats: Plant closures are the closer-to-random shock; layoffs can reflect the worker. Working-paper table; the journal abstract states the same pattern.

evidence.title: Random income shock: Florida Lottery prizes of $25,000-$50,000 vs small prizes
evidence.effect_text: A $25,000-$50,000 windfall did not change divorce rates in any meaningful way.
evidence.design: Lottery natural experiment comparing large-prize to small-prize winners
evidence.population: Florida Lottery winners
evidence.citation: Hankins, S., & Hoekstra, M. (2011). Lucky in life, unlucky in love? The effect of random income shocks on marriage and divorce. Journal of Human Resources, 46(2), 403-426.
evidence.quote: Results indicate that while positive income shocks of $25,000 to $50,000 do not cause statistically significant or economically meaningful changes in divorce rates, single women are less likely to marry as a result of the additional income.
evidence.caveats: Lottery players are not representative; windfalls differ from earned income or reduced debt. Abstract only.

evidence.design: prospective panel, discrete-time logistic
evidence.population: US first-married different-sex couples, both 18-55, PSID (1975+ cohort)
evidence.n: 6,309 couples (PSID); 1,303 divorces in 1975+ cohort, 381 in earlier cohort
evidence.citation: Killewald, A. (2016). Money, work, and marital stability: Assessing change in the gendered determinants of divorce. American Sociological Review, 81(4), 696-719.
evidence.locator: Table 3 (logistic regression of marital dissolution, PSID; columns 1. Married in 1974 or Earlier, 2. Married in 1975 or Later, 3. Pooled). Each cell prints B, (SE), OR. Value = column 2
evidence.caveats: Annual hazard OR; covariates measured in prior year.
evidence.se_or_other: SE(B) = 0.106; estimate is the printed OR; 95% CI derived as exp(ln OR +/- 1.96 x SE) (not reported).
evidence.adjusted_for: economic well-being, wife economic dependence, both spouses' FT employment, wife housework share, duration, religion, race, nativity, home ownership, children, premarital cohabitation/birth, age at marriage, each spouse's education, health, occupation/industry sex composition, region, marriage cohort

evidence.title: Earnings, net worth, debt and home ownership in SIPP couples, one year ahead (this project)
evidence.measure: change in held-out deviance (percentage points) from adding financial inputs
evidence.effect_text: Raw gradients are steep (negative net worth 24.4 vs $1M+ 4.9 separations per 1,000 couple-years), but finances add nothing to prediction once demographics are known (−0.79 points, −2.82 to +0.91).
evidence.design: Spouses linked in SIPP panels, followed one year; held-out prediction with and without financial inputs
evidence.population: US married couples, SIPP 2018-2025 year pairs
evidence.outcome: Separation or divorce within one year
evidence.citation: This project, reproducibility/sipp_marital_history/METHODS.md.
evidence.quote: **Wealth adds nothing measurable once demographics are known:** −0.79% deviance (95% CI −2.82 to +0.91) and +0.000 AUC (−0.028 to +0.026) over the demographics model on the same couples.
evidence.caveats: Wealth tracks age, marriage length and education; one-year horizon.

factors.label: Debt, wealth and money conflict
factors.decision: Paying down debt, building savings, agreeing on money
app_inputs: net worth / debt / home ownership (SIPP couples lens)
factors.direction: raw gradients steep; little independent effect once other traits and money disagreements are known
factors.size: Separation 24.4 vs 4.9 per 1,000 couple-years (negative net worth vs $1M+), but finances add nothing to held-out prediction (−0.79 points). Financial disagreements, not financial well-being, predict divorce in NSFH.
factors.causal_reading: No causal evidence that reducing debt lowers divorce risk; money conflict is a marker of relationship process.
factors.gaps: No randomised financial-stress or financial-education trial with a divorce outcome found.

evidence.title: Earnings, net worth, debt and home ownership in SIPP couples, one year ahead (this project)
evidence.measure: change in held-out deviance (percentage points) from adding financial inputs
evidence.effect_text: Raw gradients are steep (negative net worth 24.4 vs $1M+ 4.9 separations per 1,000 couple-years), but finances add nothing to prediction once demographics are known (−0.79 points, −2.82 to +0.91).
evidence.design: Spouses linked in SIPP panels, followed one year; held-out prediction with and without financial inputs
evidence.population: US married couples, SIPP 2018-2025 year pairs
evidence.outcome: Separation or divorce within one year
evidence.citation: This project, reproducibility/sipp_marital_history/METHODS.md.
evidence.quote: **Wealth adds nothing measurable once demographics are known:** −0.79% deviance (95% CI −2.82 to +0.91) and +0.000 AUC (−0.028 to +0.026) over the demographics model on the same couples.
evidence.caveats: Wealth tracks age, marriage length and education; one-year horizon.

evidence.title: Financial well-being, financial disagreements and divorce
evidence.effect_text: Financial disagreements were the strongest disagreement type predicting divorce; financial well-being itself was not associated with divorce once disagreements were modelled.
evidence.design: Longitudinal NSFH couples, hazard models with both spouses' reports
evidence.population: US married couples (National Survey of Families and Households)
evidence.citation: Dew, J., Britt, S., & Huston, S. (2012). Examining the relationship between financial issues and divorce. Family Relations, 61(4), 615-628.
evidence.quote: When financial disagreements were in the model, financial well‐being was not associated with divorce. Both wives' and husbands' financial disagreements were the strongest disagreement types to predict divorce.
evidence.caveats: Observational; disagreements may reflect relationship quality rather than money.

factors.label: Relationship / premarital education
factors.decision: Taking a relationship-education or premarital programme
app_inputs: not a model input: shown as an evidence-based option alongside the estimate
factors.direction: mixed: lower divorce in some trials, null in the two largest federal trials
factors.size: Army PREP: 7.6% vs 11.9% divorced at 2 years (8.1% vs 14.9% at the higher-risk site, null at the other); engaged/newlywed trial: 11% vs 24% dissolved at 3 years, but a one-session film-discussion arm did as well as skills training. Building Strong Families (unmarried new parents): 57.4% vs 60.5% still together at 3 years; Supporting Healthy Marriage (low-income married): 81.5% vs 81.5%. Meta-analyses: small quality gains (d about 0.06-0.36), no significant stability effect across ACF-funded programmes.
factors.causal_reading: The best-tested option in this list. Expect small gains in relationship quality; a lower divorce risk is plausible for some higher-risk married couples but is not reliable across programmes or populations.
factors.gaps: Few trials follow divorce beyond 2-3 years; most participants are white and middle-class except in the federal trials.

evidence.title: PREP (Army chaplain-delivered couple education) vs no-treatment control, both sites pooled
evidence.effect_text: Divorce by 2 years: 7.6% with PREP vs 11.9% without; odds ratio 0.60, p = .06.
evidence.design: Randomised controlled trial, intention to treat, couples nested in workshop cohorts (2-level Bernoulli model)
evidence.population: Married U.S. Army couples at two installations
evidence.n: 662 couples (343 PREP, 319 control); divorce status for 660
evidence.outcome: Filed for or obtained divorce by 2 years after the intervention
evidence.citation: Stanley, S. M., Rhoades, G. K., Loew, B. A., Allen, E. S., Carter, S., Osborne, L. J., Prentice, D., & Markman, H. J. (2014). A randomized controlled trial of relationship education in the U.S. Army: 2-year outcomes. Family Relations, 63(4), 482-495.
evidence.locator: Results, Tests Hypothesis One: Divorce Outcomes
evidence.quote: Findings from an overall test of divorce likelihood (pooled across both sites) are consistent with the prediction that the intervention group would be less likely to divorce than the control group; 7.6% (26/342) of the intervention group divorced compared to 11.9% (38/318) of the control group, B = -0.51, Odds Ratio = 0.60, p = .06.
evidence.caveats: Pooled effect is driven by Site 1; at Site 2 the intervention group divorced slightly more (6.3% vs 4.4%, OR 1.37, p = .60). No lasting effect on relationship quality.

evidence.title: PREP vs control at the higher-risk site (Site 1)
evidence.effect_text: Divorce by 2 years at the higher-risk site: 8.1% with PREP vs 14.9% without (OR 0.50).
evidence.design: Randomised controlled trial, intention to treat (site subgroup, pre-specified by the larger divorce rate)
evidence.population: Married U.S. Army couples at Site 1 (younger, lower rank, more deployments)
evidence.outcome: Filed for or obtained divorce by 2 years after the intervention
evidence.citation: Stanley, S. M., Rhoades, G. K., Loew, B. A., Allen, E. S., Carter, S., Osborne, L. J., Prentice, D., & Markman, H. J. (2014). A randomized controlled trial of relationship education in the U.S. Army: 2-year outcomes. Family Relations, 63(4), 482-495.
evidence.locator: Results, Tests Hypothesis One: Divorce Outcomes
evidence.quote: At Site 1, 8.1% (20/248) of the intervention group divorced compared to 14.9% (34/228) of the control group, B = -0.69, Odds Ratio = 0.50, p < .01.
evidence.caveats: Subgroup of a two-site trial; the effect was concentrated in ethnic-minority couples (3.8% vs 15.7%), with little difference for non-minority couples (10.6% vs 13.3%).

evidence.title: PREP for Strong Bonds (chaplain-delivered couple education) vs no-treatment control
evidence.effect_text: Divorce by 1 year: 2.0% with PREP vs 6.2% without (about 4 fewer per 100 couples).
evidence.design: Randomised controlled trial, intention to treat; couples randomised to PREP or control
evidence.population: Married U.S. Army couples (at least one spouse active duty), Site 1 of the Army PREP trial
evidence.n: 476 couples randomised at this site (248 PREP, 228 control); status known for 472
evidence.outcome: Filed for or obtained divorce by 1 year after the intervention
evidence.citation: Stanley, S. M., Allen, E. S., Markman, H. J., Rhoades, G. K., & Prentice, D. L. (2010). Decreasing divorce in Army couples: Results from a randomized controlled trial using PREP for Strong Bonds. Journal of Couple & Relationship Therapy, 9(2), 149-160.
evidence.quote: This chi-square test indicated that the PREP for Strong Bonds group had a significantly lower divorce rate (5/246 = 2.03%) than the control group (14/226 = 6.20%), χ2 (1) = 4.26, p < .05. Fisher’s exact test for significance yielded a value of p = .03.
evidence.caveats: Short follow-up; one site; superseded by the 2-year report on the full trial, where the effect held at this site but not at the second site.

evidence.title: Skills training (PREP or CARE, 15 hours) or one-session relationship awareness (watching and discussing films) vs no treatment
evidence.measure: difference in dissolution rates (treated arms minus no treatment)
evidence.effect_text: Dissolution by 3 years: 24% with no treatment vs 11% in each of PREP, CARE and relationship awareness, which did not differ.
evidence.design: Randomised trial with an assessment-only control and an active minimal (relationship awareness) arm
evidence.population: Engaged and newlywed couples, Los Angeles and Rochester
evidence.citation: Rogge, R. D., Cobb, R. J., Lawrence, E., Johnson, M. D., & Bradbury, T. N. (2013). Is skills training necessary for the primary prevention of marital distress and dissolution? A 3-year experimental study of three interventions. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 81(6), 949-961.
evidence.quote: Couples in the no-treatment condition dissolved their relationships at a higher rate (24%) than couples completing PREP, CARE, and RA, who did not differ on rates of dissolution (11%).
evidence.caveats: Small trial; the cheap one-session arm did as well as 15 hours of skills training, so the active ingredient may not be skills; skills arms had some unintended effects. Abstract only read.

evidence.title: Building Strong Families (relationship skills groups + family coordinators) vs control, pooled 8 programmes
evidence.effect_text: At 3 years 57.4% of BSF couples were still together vs 60.5% of controls (−3.2 points, p = .053); married: 20.6% vs 20.9%.
evidence.design: Federal multi-site randomised trial (Mathematica), intention to treat, regression-adjusted
evidence.population: Low-income unmarried, romantically involved couples expecting or just having had a baby
evidence.n: 5,102 couples randomised; 2,129 BSF and 2,118 control couples at 36 months
evidence.citation: Wood, R. G., Moore, Q., Clarkwest, A., Killewald, A., & Monahan, S. (2012). The long-term effects of Building Strong Families: A relationship skills education program for unmarried parents (OPRE Report 2012-28A). Washington, DC: Office of Planning, Research and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
evidence.caveats: A null-to-slightly-harmful pooled result for unmarried new parents; sites differed (Oklahoma City positive on family stability, Florida negative). Not a test for married or engaged couples.

evidence.title: Supporting Healthy Marriage (relationship and marriage education workshops + supplemental activities + family support) vs control
evidence.effect_text: 81.5% of programme couples and 81.5% of control couples were still together at 30 months: no effect on staying together.
evidence.design: Federal multi-site randomised trial (MDRC), intention to treat, regression-adjusted
evidence.population: Low-income married couples with children (8 programmes)
evidence.n: 6,298 couples randomised; 2,497 programme and 2,537 control couples at 30 months
evidence.outcome: Still married (or in a committed relationship with the same partner) at 30 months
evidence.citation: Lundquist, E., Hsueh, J., Lowenstein, A. E., Faucetta, K., Gubits, D., Michalopoulos, C., & Knox, V. (2014). A family-strengthening program for low-income families: Final impacts from the Supporting Healthy Marriage evaluation (OPRE Report 2014-09A). Washington, DC: Office of Planning, Research and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
evidence.caveats: Small positive effects on relationship quality (see SHM2014_30mo_happiness) did not translate into stability. Precise null: the CI excludes effects larger than about 2 points.

evidence.title: Marriage and relationship education (MRE), all programmes
evidence.measure: Cohen's d range across experimental-study estimates
evidence.effect_text: Relationship quality d = .30 to .36; communication d = .43 to .45. Stability was rarely measured.
evidence.design: Meta-analysis of 117 studies (86 reports); range shown is for experimental (controlled) studies
evidence.population: Mostly white, middle-class couples
evidence.citation: Hawkins, A. J., Blanchard, V. L., Baldwin, S. A., & Fawcett, E. B. (2008). Does marriage and relationship education work? A meta-analytic study. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 76(5), 723-734.
evidence.quote: The effect sizes for relationship quality for experimental studies ranged from d = .30 to .36, while the communication skills effect sizes ranged from d = .43 to .45.
evidence.caveats: Little racial or economic diversity; relationship stability and aggression rarely measured.

evidence.title: Couple and relationship education for lower-income participants
evidence.effect_text: Small effect, d = .061 overall in controlled studies, vs d = .352 in one-group pre/post studies.
evidence.design: Meta-analysis of 38 studies (47 samples); estimate is for control-group studies
evidence.population: Samples with more than two-thirds below twice the poverty level
evidence.citation: Hawkins, A. J., & Erickson, S. E. (2015). Is couple and relationship education effective for lower income participants? A meta-analytic study. Journal of Family Psychology, 29(1), 59-68.
evidence.quote: Overall effect sizes for control-group studies suggest that CRE for diverse, lower income couples has small, positive relationship effects (overall d = .061)
evidence.caveats: Uncontrolled pre/post designs overstate effects about six-fold relative to controlled designs.

evidence.title: ACF-funded Healthy Marriage and Relationship Education programmes
evidence.measure: Cohen's d for couple relationship quality
evidence.effect_text: Relationship quality d = .114; effects on relationship stability were not significant.
evidence.design: Meta-analysis of 32 control-group evaluations of federally funded programmes
evidence.population: Lower-income couples in ACF-funded programmes
evidence.citation: Hawkins, A. J., Hokanson, S., Loveridge, E., Milius, E., Duncan, M., Booth, M., & Pollard, B. (2022). How effective are ACF-funded couple relationship education programs? A meta-analytic study. Family Process, 61(3), 970-985.
evidence.quote: Overall, our review of 32 control-group studies found a range of small but significant effects for couple relationship quality (d = .114), relationship skills (d = .132), mental health (d = .074), and coparenting (d = .033), but non-significant effects for relationship stability, parenting, and child well-being.
evidence.caveats: Pooled across heterogeneous programmes; stability effect reported only as non-significant in the abstract.

evidence.title: Premarital prevention programmes
evidence.effect_text: Mean effect size .80 for short-term outcomes; long-term effects (including divorce) unknown.
evidence.design: Meta-analytic review of premarital programme outcome studies
evidence.population: Engaged / premarital couples
evidence.outcome: Immediate and short-term interpersonal skills and relationship quality
evidence.citation: Carroll, J. S., & Doherty, W. J. (2003). Evaluating the effectiveness of premarital prevention programs: A meta-analytic review of outcome research. Family Relations, 52(2), 105-118.
evidence.quote: Results revealed that the mean effect size for premarital programs was .80 ... However, because of a lack of extended follow‐up research, conclusions about long‐term effectiveness remain elusive.
evidence.caveats: Older, smaller studies; includes non-randomised designs; the authors say long-term effectiveness remains elusive. Later meta-analyses find much smaller controlled effects.

evidence.title: Self-selected participation in premarital education
evidence.effect_text: People who had premarital education reported better marriages and lower odds of divorce.
evidence.design: Random household telephone survey; retrospective report of premarital education
evidence.population: Adults in Oklahoma, Kansas, Arkansas and Texas
evidence.outcome: Marital quality and odds of divorce
evidence.citation: Stanley, S. M., Amato, P. R., Johnson, C. A., & Markman, H. J. (2006). Premarital education, marital quality, and marital stability: Findings from a large, random household survey. Journal of Family Psychology, 20(1), 117-126.
evidence.quote: although survey methods allow only weak inferences about causal relations ... participation in premarital education was associated with higher levels of satisfaction and commitment in marriage and lower levels of conflict-and also reduced odds of divorce.
evidence.caveats: People choose premarital education (often through a religious congregation); the authors note surveys allow only weak causal inference.

factors.label: Couples counselling / therapy
app_inputs: not a model input: shown as an evidence-based option alongside the estimate
factors.direction: better relationship satisfaction; effect on divorce vs no therapy not established
factors.size: Behavioural couple therapy vs no treatment: d = 0.585 (30 RCTs). After 5 years, about 1 in 4 seriously distressed couples had separated after either of two good therapies (25.7% IBCT, 27.9% TBCT); about half improved meaningfully.
factors.causal_reading: Strong evidence that therapy improves satisfaction for distressed couples; no trial compares divorce with an untreated group over years, so a divorce-risk number for therapy would be invented.
factors.gaps: No long-term RCT with an untreated control and a divorce outcome found; no model has strong support by Chambless criteria.

evidence.title: Behavioural marital therapy vs no treatment
evidence.effect_text: d = .585 vs no treatment; possible publication bias (missing small null studies) may inflate it.
evidence.design: Meta-analysis of 30 randomised experiments against no-treatment controls
evidence.population: Distressed couples
evidence.citation: Shadish, W. R., & Baldwin, S. A. (2005). Effects of behavioral marital therapy: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 73(1), 6-14.
evidence.quote: Results showed that behavioral marital therapy is significantly more effective than no treatment (d=.585).
evidence.caveats: Outcome is satisfaction, not separation; possible small-study publication bias.

evidence.title: Couple therapy (all modalities)
evidence.effect_text: Satisfaction improves by g = 1.12 in therapy vs g = 0.12 (not significant) on waitlists.
evidence.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of 58 studies (40 samples, 2,092 couples); estimate is the within-group pre-post gain
evidence.population: Distressed opposite-sex couples
evidence.outcome: Relationship satisfaction, pre to post (within group)
evidence.citation: Roddy, M. K., Walsh, L. M., Rothman, K., Hatch, S. G., & Doss, B. D. (2020). Meta-analysis of couple therapy: Effects across outcomes, designs, timeframes, and other moderators. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 88(7), 583-596.
evidence.quote: Couple therapy has a large effect on relationship satisfaction (pre to post within-group Hedges ḡ = 1.12, CI [0.92, 1.31], p < .001) and couples assigned to waitlists do not significantly improve (pre-to-post within-group satisfaction Hedges ḡ = 0.12, CI [-0.04, 0.29], p > .05).
evidence.caveats: Within-group gains overstate the between-group effect; separation not pooled; opposite-sex couples only.

evidence.title: Integrative (IBCT) vs traditional (TBCT) behavioural couple therapy, about 8 months
evidence.effect_text: About 1 in 4 seriously distressed couples had separated or divorced 5 years after either therapy (25.7% IBCT, 27.9% TBCT); about half improved meaningfully in satisfaction.
evidence.design: Randomised trial of two active therapies (no untreated control), 5-year follow-up
evidence.population: Chronically and seriously distressed married couples, Los Angeles and Seattle
evidence.citation: Christensen, A., Atkins, D. C., Baucom, B., & Yi, J. (2010). Marital status and satisfaction five years following a randomized clinical trial comparing traditional versus integrative behavioral couple therapy. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 78(2), 225-235.
evidence.quote: Relationship status, obtained on all 134 couples, revealed that 25.7% of IBCT couples and 27.9% of TBCT couples were separated or divorced.
evidence.caveats: No untreated control, so the trial cannot say whether therapy lowers divorce compared with no therapy; it shows what happens after good therapy for severely distressed couples.

evidence.title: Emotionally focused couple therapy (EFT)
evidence.effect_text: d = 1.31 across four small trials; a 2020 review finds no significant difference between EFT and cognitive-behavioural couple therapy.
evidence.design: Meta-analysis of four randomised trials (as reported by a later review)
evidence.population: Distressed couples
evidence.citation: Johnson, S. M., Hunsley, J., Greenberg, L., & Schindler, D. (1999). Emotionally focused couples therapy: Status and challenges. Clinical Psychology: Science and Practice, 6(1), 67-79. (Figure as reported by Bodenmann, G., Kessler, M., Kuhn, R., Hocker, L., & Randall, A. K. (2020). Cognitive-behavioral and emotion-focused couple therapy: Similarities and differences. Clinical Psychology in Europe, 2(3), e2741.)
evidence.quote: In the meta-analysis by Johnson et al. (1999), including four randomized trials, an effect size of d = 1.31 is reported.
evidence.caveats: Secondhand figure; four small trials, mostly by the developers; satisfaction, not separation.

evidence.title: Empirically supported couple therapy models (Chambless criteria)
evidence.effect_text: No couple therapy model met the bar for strong support; seven (including behavioural, EFT, Gottman and IBCT) had modest support.
evidence.design: Systematic review of 40 eligible studies against APA Chambless criteria
evidence.population: Couples with relationship distress
evidence.outcome: Strength of empirical support per therapy model
evidence.citation: Jackson, J. B., Codecá, L., Miller, R. B., Simpson, J. E., O'Leary, A. M., & Renner, S. M. (2026). Empirically supported couple therapy models for couple relationship distress: A replication and update. Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 52(4), e70162.
evidence.quote: Applying these criteria to 40 eligible studies, we found that, in contrast to Baucom and colleagues, no couple therapy models met the standards for strong empirical support; insufficient sample size and lack of independent replication were the most frequent limitations. Seven models demonstrated modest support
evidence.caveats: Abstract only; criteria reward replication and sample size, not effect on divorce.

factors.label: Conflict behaviour
factors.decision: Changing how you argue (destructive conflict, hostility, money fights)
app_inputs: newlywed lens: hostility and conflict questions
factors.size: Husband's destructive conflict at year 1: HR 4.28 per scale point (time-varying); wife's 1.51. Changing conflict through skills training: SHM reduced negative behaviour without changing stability; skills training did no better than a one-session awareness arm.
factors.causal_reading: Destructive conflict is a strong prospective marker. Experiments that change conflict skills improve communication but have not shown that this is what lowers divorce.
factors.gaps: Gottman-style accuracy claims are in-sample (see literature evidence); no trial isolates conflict change as the mechanism.

evidence.design: prospective Cox regression
evidence.population: Early Years of Marriage Project, Wayne County MI, 47% White / 53% Black
evidence.citation: Birditt, K. S., Brown, E., Orbuch, T. L., & McIlvane, J. M. (2010). Marital conflict behaviors and implications for divorce over 16 years. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(5), 1188-1204.
evidence.locator: Table 3 (Cox regression, Year 1 conflict behaviours; n = 207): columns Model 1 Block 1, Model 1 Block 2, Model 2, Model 3, Model 4; value = Model 1 Block 2
evidence.quote: Cox Regression Models Examining Divorce as a Function of Conflict Behaviors in Year 1 (n = 207) ... Destructive | | | | | ... Husband | | 4.28** | 6.37** | | ... Hus. Destructive X Years to divorce | | .14** | .13** | |
evidence.caveats: Scale-unit HR (not standardised); time-varying effect for husband; self-report.
evidence.se_or_other: p < .01; no CI or SE printed. Per 1-point higher husband score on a 1-4 scale (mean of: yelled and shouted, insulted or called names, brought up things from long ago, had to have the last word). The same model carries a proportional-hazards correction "Hus. Destructive X Years to divorce" HR .14, i.e. the husband effect is time-varying and 4.28 is not a constant hazard ratio.
evidence.adjusted_for: couple income, education, income ratio, premarital children, months cohabited, couple age, each spouse raised with 2 parents, race

evidence.unit: per 1 point on the 1-4 destructive-behaviour scale
evidence.design: prospective Cox
evidence.population: Early Years of Marriage Project
evidence.citation: Birditt, K. S., Brown, E., Orbuch, T. L., & McIlvane, J. M. (2010). Marital conflict behaviors and implications for divorce over 16 years. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(5), 1188-1204.
evidence.locator: Table 3 (Cox regression, Year 1 conflict behaviours; n = 207): columns Model 1 Block 1, Model 1 Block 2, Model 2, Model 3, Model 4; value = Model 1 Block 2 (all four behaviour types for both spouses plus race, couple education, income, income ratio, premarital children, months cohabited, age at marriage, parents' family structure)
evidence.caveats: Self-report; unit HR.
evidence.se_or_other: p < .05; no CI or SE printed. Per 1-point higher wife score on a 1-4 scale (same four items). Year 1 wife means printed in Table 2: 2.0 (White) and 2.2 (Black), SD .8. No time interaction reported for wives.

evidence.title: Financial well-being, financial disagreements and divorce
evidence.effect_text: Financial disagreements were the strongest disagreement type predicting divorce; financial well-being itself was not associated with divorce once disagreements were modelled.
evidence.design: Longitudinal NSFH couples, hazard models with both spouses' reports
evidence.population: US married couples (National Survey of Families and Households)
evidence.citation: Dew, J., Britt, S., & Huston, S. (2012). Examining the relationship between financial issues and divorce. Family Relations, 61(4), 615-628.
evidence.quote: When financial disagreements were in the model, financial well‐being was not associated with divorce. Both wives' and husbands' financial disagreements were the strongest disagreement types to predict divorce.
evidence.caveats: Observational; disagreements may reflect relationship quality rather than money.

evidence.title: Skills training (PREP or CARE, 15 hours) or one-session relationship awareness (watching and discussing films) vs no treatment
evidence.measure: difference in dissolution rates (treated arms minus no treatment)
evidence.effect_text: Dissolution by 3 years: 24% with no treatment vs 11% in each of PREP, CARE and relationship awareness, which did not differ.
evidence.design: Randomised trial with an assessment-only control and an active minimal (relationship awareness) arm
evidence.population: Engaged and newlywed couples, Los Angeles and Rochester
evidence.citation: Rogge, R. D., Cobb, R. J., Lawrence, E., Johnson, M. D., & Bradbury, T. N. (2013). Is skills training necessary for the primary prevention of marital distress and dissolution? A 3-year experimental study of three interventions. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 81(6), 949-961.
evidence.quote: Couples in the no-treatment condition dissolved their relationships at a higher rate (24%) than couples completing PREP, CARE, and RA, who did not differ on rates of dissolution (11%).
evidence.caveats: Small trial; the cheap one-session arm did as well as 15 hours of skills training, so the active ingredient may not be skills; skills arms had some unintended effects. Abstract only read.

evidence.title: PREP (5 sessions of communication and conflict-management training) vs control, premarital couples
evidence.effect_text: At 5 years, PREP couples had better communication and less marital violence than controls.
evidence.design: Controlled trial with matched assignment; couples who declined the programme analysed separately (not a clean randomised comparison)
evidence.population: Couples planning marriage, Denver
evidence.outcome: Communication and marital violence at 4-5 years
evidence.citation: Markman, H. J., Renick, M. J., Floyd, F. J., Stanley, S. M., & Clements, M. (1993). Preventing marital distress through communication and conflict management training: A 4- and 5-year follow-up. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 61(1), 70-77.
evidence.quote: At the 5-year follow-up, intervention, as compared with control, couples had higher levels of positive and lower levels of negative communication skills and lower levels of marital violence.
evidence.caveats: Selection effects among decliners acknowledged by the authors; abstract only.

evidence.title: Supporting Healthy Marriage: relationship happiness
evidence.measure: impact on a 1-7 scale (effect size 0.13 SD)
evidence.effect_text: Happiness 5.94 vs 5.79 on a 1-7 scale (effect size 0.13); "marriage in trouble" 42.8% vs 47.3%.
evidence.design: Federal multi-site randomised trial (MDRC)
evidence.population: Low-income married couples with children
evidence.outcome: Couple's average relationship happiness (1-7 scale) at 30 months
evidence.citation: Lundquist, E., Hsueh, J., Lowenstein, A. E., Faucetta, K., Gubits, D., Michalopoulos, C., & Knox, V. (2014). A family-strengthening program for low-income families: Final impacts from the Supporting Healthy Marriage evaluation (OPRE Report 2014-09A). Washington, DC: Office of Planning, Research and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
evidence.quote: Couple’s average report of relationship happinessb 5.94 5.79 0.15 0.13 *** 0.03
evidence.caveats: Self-reported; small effects; no effect on staying married.
